title: Discovery Channel's Expedition X seeks to uncover ghosts of Guam
excerpt: Discovery Channel’s Expedition X featured Guam on one of its latest episodes, which sought to explore paranormal activity tied to the island’s history and culture.
content:
Discovery Channel’s Expedition X featured Guam on one of its latest episodes, which sought to explore paranormal activity tied to the island’s history and culture.

The episode, “Ghosts of Guam,” aired on Sept. 10.

The show’s field biologist Phil Torres and paranormal researcher Heather Amaro visit the island to address reports of shadow figures, phantom battle sounds, full-body apparitions of soldiers, and “ancient spirits that are causing chaos,” referring to the taotao mo’na.

The group’s trip examined the centuries of conflict on the island, starting from the Spanish Colonial era to World War II.

Upon arriving on the island, Torres, Amaro, and the show’s production team were treated to a cultural performance, welcoming them at the Valley of the Latte Adventure Park in Talo’fo’fo’.

‘Soaked in blood’

Expedition X’s host Josh Gates described the 10-day conflict on Guam during World War II as intense and brutal for U.S. and Japanese forces.

On July 21, 1944, U.S. forces landed on the beaches of Asan, pushing the Japanese garrison further and further into the island’s interior.

Each inch of ground the U.S. gained in the conflict was “soaked in blood,” Gates said. More than 17,000 Japanese soldiers, around 1,100 CHamorus, and 1,700 U.S. soldiers were killed over the Battle of Guam, he said.

Since then, residents reported seeing ghosts in the jungle, lights, and disembodied voices.

“Some believe the fallen soldiers never left,” Gates narrated.

Torres and Amaro met with local Sean Monforte as the chosen subject matter expert on the Asan conflict.

Monforte told the investigators that more than 1,000 U.S. Marines died taking Asan beach and pointed to pill boxes and caves Japanese defenders used to attempt to fight them off.

“It was a very bloody battle,” he said. “We were caught between the bombings and the Japanese brutality.”

Monforte said residents have heard and witnessed phantom explosions and vehicles and seen what he described as “lantern lights” along the ridgeline of Asan Beach Unit at night where following it leads to seeing a Japanese soldier running into the many caves and outcroppings.

He described a personal encounter where he and his friend were driving in the car and saw a Japanese soldier in full uniform in the rearview mirror. The encounter led the two to abandon the vehicle out of fear.

“That car was never driven by myself again,” Monforte said.

Torres and Amaro camped out at night in Asan, experiencing what they said, “100% was someone’s voice.” It was later determined to be a migratory sea bird.

At one of the WWII pillboxes, Amaro attempted to trigger paranormal activity using Morse code through a World War II signal lamp. Separately, Torres spotted what appeared to be one of the “lantern lights.”

The team picked up a faint rhythm, while mostly meaningless, they were able to determine a message of “V” which they understood as victory. A letter “V” transmission in the military according to Gates, was the same message they used after taking Asan.

The duo investigated and stumbled upon a cave where Torres suffered a near-medical episode, likely due to dehydration, but Amaro took it as a sign of a taotao mo’na encounter.

Amaro used a World War II-era antenna attached to their spirit box, a device that scans radio frequencies that’s believed to be used to talk to spirits.

They received a response that said, “I’m here” and told the investigators that they were a resident that were killed in the cave.

The people of before

Torres spoked to Michael Bevacqua, curator for the Guam Museum, to learn more about the taotao mo’na following their alleged encounter at Asan.

Bevacqua explained the taotao mo’na are the ancestral spirits of the CHamorus that seek balance and respect in nature.

“[They’re] always reminding people, ‘Don’t take too much, don’t take more than what you need’,” he said.

Conflict and colonialism threw nature out of balance on Guam, Bevacqua said.

“I imagine they’re pretty angry.”

Bevacqua said that taotao mo’na could cause disorientation and sickness if they feel that they are disrespected.

Amaro met with Barbara Villagomez, a nature guide who had an encounter with the taotao mo’na.

Villagomez told Amaro that she and three other hikers were “turned around multiple times” in the jungle.

“It didn’t matter we had GPS on, it wasn’t working for us,” she said.

Tearful, Villagomez said she knew it was taotao mo’na telling the group that they weren’t wanted there.

She asked the taotao mo’na for forgiveness and the group was eventually able to find their way out in an area miles away from where they started.

“You got to be really careful. Respect the taotao mo’na,” Villagomez said.

Bevacqua said there are certain areas around the island, rich in history, where taotao mo’na reside. He pointed to the latte stones as one of those places.

Latte stones were the foundations of the homes of ancient CHamorus that allowed them to bury the dead beneath the residents.

“Find the latte stones, find the taotao mo’na,” Torres affirmed.

Bevacqua warned that the taking of artifacts from the ancient latte sites could lead to punishment.

‘Strangest nights of odd things happening’

The duo paddled up the Talo’fo’fo’ river to one of the few remaining undisturbed latte stone sites on the island.

Once night fell, they found several latte stones where they set up their lights and trail cameras.

Amaro attempted to invoke a response through water scrying. She explained that the likely village was set up near the river because of access to water.

Water scrying involves asking spirits questions while gently stirring water in a bowl with the response appearing in the bowl. The team reviewed the results frame by frame using a camera.

An analysis of the images showed a “flurry of unusual shapes in the water” after being asked if they could show themselves.

Amaro said they appeared to look like faces and symbols seen in ancient CHamoru petroglyphs.

Torres came across what appeared to be a piece of ancient CHamoru pottery.

“Someone over a thousand years ago may have had this in their home,” he explained. And the person might have been buried somewhere nearby.

That piece was able to positively identified the piece as an artifact likely crafted some 1,000 years ago, according to Gates.

A noise in the darkness caused him to run after it and was “turned around” ending up where he started.

Torres’s GPS tracker on his watch indicated that he had been circling the area, despite him stating that he was heading in a straight line.

Over the radio, Amaro said this could be a warning from the taotao mo’na and told him he needs to ask for forgiveness.

Torres asked for forgiveness: “Taotao mo’na, if you’re out here listening, I would like to ask for forgiveness for anything I may have done. [May] you please help me find my way back to the latte stones.”

He was then subsequently reunited with Amaro.

“This was one of the strangest nights of odd things happening,” he said.

Amaro attempted to communicate with the “four classical elements:” water, fire, air, and earth. She placed soil in her bowl of water and floated a lit candle and spoke into it.

She asked whether there was taotao mo’na present, the flame of the candle moving intensely indicated “yes”.

Torres asked whether his sickness at Asan and him becoming lost was due to them and what appeared to be intense activity of the flame again indicated a “yes” response.

The taotao mo’na also indicated that people are taking too much from the land and that imbalance is the reason why it’s making its presence more known.

The taotao mo’na indicated that it wanted respect, not fear.

You can watch Expedition X on Discovery Channel and through Discovery’s streaming platforms.
